lesson_title: The Goat, the Ropes and the Echo
hook_text: Tie a goat outside a round kraal with two ropes touching the wall. The ropes are ALWAYS equal — and that's an exam theorem.
clip_script: Tie a goat to one peg outside a perfectly round kraal, with two ropes running from the peg to just touch the wall — one on each side. Here's the theorem: those two ropes are exactly equal. Always. Move the peg anywhere you like — still twins. Why? The line from the peg to the centre of the kraal is a mirror, and each rope is the other one's reflection. Now watch this buy you exam marks. Twins make an isosceles triangle: peg, touch point, touch point. Say the angle at the peg is forty degrees. The other two angles split what's left of one eighty — seventy each. And now the beautiful part, the tangent-chord theorem: that seventy, sitting between the rope and the wall's chord, echoes straight across the chord to the far side of the circle. Someone standing on the opposite arc, looking at the same chord, sees exactly seventy degrees. Shout at the wall, and the far side hears it perfectly. Twin ropes. Isosceles payout. Echo across. Three sentences — and that's a five-mark rider from Paper 2, solved at walking pace.
visual_style: A hand-drawn kraal from above, a goat at a peg with two taut ropes touching the circular wall; a mirror line flashing through peg and centre; the 40-70-70 triangle lighting up; the 70 rippling across the chord like a sound wave to the far arc.
mood: Warm, rural, quietly triumphant — farm picture becomes exam weapon.
pacing: Gentle setup with the goat, a beat on 'Always.', building speed through the triangle to the echo reveal.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and walk into the tangent theorems with pictures instead of panic.
